Seattle School District No. 1 (2007), the Supreme Court held that the use of race as a tiebreaker in student assignment plans was not narrowly tailored to achieve a compelling interest, emphasizing that race-based decisions must be subject to strict scrutiny and that less restrictive means must be considered.

The Supreme Court has consistently held that race-based government action is subject to strict scrutiny, requiring the government to prove that the action is narrowly tailored to achieve a compelling governmental interest.

In Fisher I, the Court explicitly stated that the burden of proof remains on the university to demonstrate that no workable race-neutral alternatives would produce the educational benefits of diversity.

The University of Texas at Austin had implemented a 'Top 10 Percent' plan which guaranteed admission to students in the top 10% of their high school class, which the university argued provided sufficient diversity without the need for race-conscious admissions.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause of the U.S. Constitution (Article IV, Section 1) requires each state to recognize the public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of every other state.

In the 1994 case of Baker v. General Motors Corp., the Supreme Court held that a state court judgment is entitled to full faith and credit in other states, and that a state cannot refuse to enforce a judgment from another state simply because it disagrees with the underlying reasoning or policy.

In the 1996 case of Franchise Tax Board of California v. Hyatt, the Supreme Court discussed the scope of the Full Faith and Credit Clause, noting that while states have some discretion, they cannot refuse to enforce judgments from sister states based on public policy objections.

The Supreme Court has historically applied the Full Faith and Credit Clause to family law matters, including custody and divorce decrees, requiring states to recognize valid judgments from other states even if the underlying facts or laws differ.

In the case of V.L. v. E.L., the Alabama Court of Civil Appeals refused to recognize a same-sex adoption decree issued by a Georgia court, reasoning that the Georgia court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because Georgia law did not permit same-sex adoption at the time.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in V.L. v. E.L. on October 5, 2015, to resolve a circuit split regarding whether the Full Faith and Credit Clause requires a state to recognize a judgment from another state when the rendering court's jurisdiction is challenged based on the public policy of the enforcing state.

In the 2015 case of Williams v. North Carolina, the Supreme Court established that a state court's determination of its own jurisdiction is generally entitled to full faith and credit in other states, unless the rendering court clearly lacked jurisdiction under its own laws.

In 2022, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Department of Education v. Brown to review the Fifth Circuit's decision that the Department of Education lacked statutory authority to implement the Borrower Defense to Repayment rule changes under the Higher Education Act.

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, in its decision issued in 2022, held that the Department of Education's 2016 Borrower Defense rule and subsequent 2022 interim final rule exceeded the agency's statutory authority under the Higher Education Act because the statute did not explicitly grant the power to discharge loans based on institutional misconduct.

In Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (1984), the Supreme Court established a two-step framework for reviewing agency statutory interpretations, where courts must defer to an agency's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous statute it administers.

In Massachusetts v. EPA (2007), the Supreme Court held that the EPA's interpretation of the Clean Air Act's definition of 'air pollutant' was reasonable and entitled to deference, reinforcing the principle that agencies have broad discretion to interpret ambiguous statutory terms within their expertise.

In Gundy v. United States (2019), a plurality of the Supreme Court upheld the delegation of authority to the Attorney General to set guidelines for the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act, with Justice Kagan's plurality opinion emphasizing that broad delegations are permissible if there is an 'intelligible principle' to guide the agency.

In 2022, the Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Department of Education v. Brown, where the government argued that the Higher Education Act's general grant of authority to the Secretary of Education to 'administer' the Act includes the power to implement borrower defense provisions, while the respondents argued that such a significant power requires explicit statutory authorization.

In West Virginia v. EPA (2022), the Supreme Court applied the 'major questions doctrine,' holding that an agency cannot assert expansive authority over issues of vast economic and political significance without clear congressional authorization, even if the statute is ambiguous.

In 2021, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Oral Surgeons, P.C. v. Cincinnati Insurance Co. to address whether a state court's interpretation of an insurance policy's 'occurrence' definition, which excluded intentional acts, violated the McCarran-Ferguson Act's prohibition on federal preemption of state insurance regulation.

The McCarran-Ferguson Act, 15 U.S.C. § 1011 et seq., provides that the business of insurance is subject to state law and that no federal law shall be construed to invalidate, impair, or supersede any state law enacted for the regulation of the business of insurance unless the federal law specifically relates to the business of insurance.

In Rumsfeld v. FAIR (2006), the Supreme Court held that the First Amendment does not compel the government to subsidize speech it disagrees with, but this case is distinct as it involves statutory preemption rather than constitutional free speech.

In Metropolitan Life Insurance Co. v. Massachusetts (1985), the Supreme Court held that the McCarran-Ferguson Act does not preempt state laws that regulate the business of insurance, even if those laws have an economic impact on insurance companies, unless the state law is not specifically directed at the insurance industry.

The Supreme Court has historically shown deference to state court interpretations of insurance contracts under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, viewing the Act as a strong barrier to federal preemption of state insurance regulation.

The petitioner, Oral Surgeons, P.C., argued that the state court's interpretation of the policy was effectively a federal common law rule that should preempt state law, but the Supreme Court has generally rejected such arguments when the state law is a valid exercise of the state's police power over insurance.

35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(1) imposes liability on a person who supplies from the United States components of a patented invention for combination outside the United States, specifically regarding the supply of 'all or a substantial portion of the components' of such invention.

In Microsoft Corp. v. AT&T Corp. (2007), the Supreme Court held that a single software component, even if copied from the United States and installed on a foreign hard drive, does not constitute 'all or a substantial portion' of the components of a patented invention under § 271(f)(1) because the software itself is intangible and the physical copies were made abroad.

In Microsoft Corp. v. AT&T Corp. (2007), the Supreme Court further clarified that the phrase 'all or a substantial portion' refers to the number and importance of components, and that a single component, even if essential, is not a 'substantial portion' of the invention.

The Federal Circuit, in Life Technologies Corp. v. Promega Corp. (2014), held that a single component (a primer) supplied from the United States could constitute a 'substantial portion' of the components of a patented invention under § 271(f)(1) if that component was essential to the invention's function.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Life Technologies Corp. v. Promega Corp. to resolve a circuit split regarding whether a single component can ever constitute a 'substantial portion' of the components of a patented invention under § 271(f)(1).

In Microsoft Corp. v. AT&T Corp. (2007), the Court emphasized that the statutory language 'all or a substantial portion' implies a quantitative and qualitative assessment, but the Court in that case focused on the intangible nature of software and the fact that the copies were made abroad, leaving open the question of physical components.

The Federal Circuit in Life Technologies (2014) relied on the qualitative importance of the single component (a primer) to find liability, diverging from the quantitative approach suggested by the Microsoft decision's discussion of 'substantial portion'.

In Seila Law LLC v. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (2020), the Supreme Court held that the CFPB's single-director structure was unconstitutional because the director could only be removed for cause, violating the separation of powers.

In Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010), the Supreme Court held that the dual-layer for-cause removal protection for PCAOB members was unconstitutional because it insulated officials from both Presidential and Senate oversight.

In Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935), the Supreme Court established that Congress may limit the President's removal power for officers of independent agencies who perform quasi-legislative or quasi-judicial functions, provided they are not purely executive officers.

The Federal Reserve Board members are protected by a for-cause removal standard (for 'inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office') under the Federal Reserve Act, a structure that had not been struck down by the Supreme Court prior to 2021.

In Collins v. Yellen, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals held that the for-cause removal protection for Federal Reserve Board members was unconstitutional under the reasoning of Seila Law and Free Enterprise Fund, and that the entire Federal Reserve Act was severable from the unconstitutional removal provision.

In Seila Law, the Court explicitly distinguished the CFPB from the Federal Reserve, noting that the Federal Reserve's structure includes a Board of Governors with multiple members and a different removal standard, suggesting the Court might view the Federal Reserve's structure as distinct from the single-director CFPB.

The Supreme Court has historically been reluctant to invalidate entire statutory schemes based on a single structural defect unless the defect is inextricably linked to the statute's operation, often preferring to sever the unconstitutional provision.

In Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010), the Supreme Court held that the for-cause removal protection for members of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board violated the separation of powers because it impeded the President's ability to supervise executive officers.

In Commodity Futures Trading Commission v. Schor (1986), the Supreme Court held that the creation of an Article I tribunal with limited jurisdiction to adjudicate state law counterclaims did not violate Article III, emphasizing a functional approach to separation of powers.

In Mistretta v. United States (1989), the Supreme Court upheld the Sentencing Commission as an independent agency within the judicial branch, finding that the delegation of rulemaking authority to the Commission did not violate the non-delegation doctrine or separation of powers.

In American Trucking Associations v. Smith (1990), the Supreme Court held that the Federal Railroad Administration's regulation of railroad hours of service was a valid exercise of congressional power under the Commerce Clause.

The statutory scheme in question (the Rail Passenger Service Act amendments) required Amtrak, a quasi-public corporation, to develop performance metrics and standards that the Department of Transportation would enforce, raising the question of whether Amtrak's participation in rulemaking constituted private action or government action subject to constitutional constraints.

In Dames & Moore v. Regan (1981), the Supreme Court recognized that the President and Congress have broad authority to manage foreign affairs and economic sanctions, often upholding executive actions that blend private and public interests.

In FCC v. League of Women Voters (1984), the Supreme Court struck down a provision prohibiting non-commercial educational broadcast stations from editorializing, finding it violated the First Amendment, but the Court also discussed the limits of government regulation of private entities.

The D.C. Circuit in Association of American Railroads v. DOT (2013) held that the statutory scheme violated the non-delegation doctrine and the separation of powers by delegating legislative power to a private entity (Amtrak) and by allowing private entities to participate in the creation of binding regulations without sufficient executive oversight.

In Niz-Chavez v. Garland, the petitioner, a lawful permanent resident, was served with a Notice to Appear (NTA) that did not specify the time and place of his removal hearing, which was provided in a separate document later.

The statutory provision at issue, 8 U.S.C. § 1229a(b)(1), requires that a Notice to Appear contain specific information including the time and place of the hearing, and the statute defines the 'stop-time rule' for cancellation of removal as ceasing when the alien is served with a Notice to Appear.

In Paredes-Uribe v. Holder, 663 F.3d 800 (9th Cir. 2011), the Ninth Circuit held that a Notice to Appear that does not include the time and place of the hearing is defective and does not trigger the stop-time rule.

In contrast, the Fifth Circuit in United States v. Lopez, 873 F.3d 235 (5th Cir. 2017), held that the stop-time rule is triggered by the service of the initial Notice to Appear even if it lacks the time and place details, which are provided later.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Niz-Chavez v. Garland on October 16, 2020, to resolve the circuit split regarding whether the stop-time rule is triggered by a defective Notice to Appear.

The text of the statute uses the singular 'a notice to appear' in the phrase 'served with a notice to appear,' which suggests that the notice must contain all required elements at the time of service to be considered 'a notice to appear' under the statute.
The Government argued that the stop-time rule is triggered by the initial document, regardless of missing information, to promote administrative efficiency and finality in removal proceedings.
The petitioner argued that the statutory text requires a complete notice to trigger the stop-time rule, and that a fragmented notice does not satisfy the statutory definition.

In 2019, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Holleman v. Zatecky to review whether the district court's denial of a motion to disqualify counsel, based on a conflict of interest arising from the attorney's prior representation of a co-defendant, was an abuse of discretion.

The underlying case involved a civil rights action where the petitioner, Robert Holleman, alleged that his trial counsel was disqualified because the attorney had previously represented a co-defendant in a related matter, creating a potential conflict of interest under the Sixth Amendment and ethical rules.

In United States v. Cronic, 466 U.S. 648 (1984), the Supreme Court held that a Sixth Amendment violation occurs only if counsel's performance was so deficient that it deprived the defendant of a fair trial, or if there was a complete denial of counsel, but generally requires a showing of actual prejudice or specific circumstances where prejudice is presumed.

In Strickland v. Washington, 466 U.S. 668 (1984), the Court established a two-prong test for ineffective assistance of counsel claims: the defendant must show that counsel's performance was deficient and that the deficiency prejudiced the defense.

In United States v. Gonzalez-Lopez, 548 U.S. 140 (2006), the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel of choice is a structural error that does not require a showing of prejudice, but this right is not absolute and can be limited by valid conflict of interest rules.

The Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals, in its decision below, affirmed the district court's denial of the motion to disqualify, finding that the petitioner failed to demonstrate a significant risk of prejudice or a violation of the Sixth Amendment rights.

The Supreme Court has historically been reluctant to overturn lower court determinations regarding the disqualification of counsel unless there is a clear abuse of discretion or a fundamental constitutional violation, as seen in cases like Wainwright v. Sykes, 433 U.S. 72 (1977), which emphasized the finality of state court judgments and the high bar for federal habeas relief.

In 2016, the Supreme Court decided Kisor v. Wilkie (then Kisor v. Shulkin), a case involving the interpretation of the Social Security Administration's own regulations, where the Court emphasized that agencies must interpret their own regulations consistently and that deference is not automatic if the regulation is ambiguous.

The Supreme Court has established in cases like Barnhart v. Walton (2002) that courts must defer to an agency's reasonable interpretation of its own ambiguous regulations under the framework of Auer deference (later refined in Kisor).

In the case of Hargress v. Social Security Administration, the petitioner challenged the Social Security Administration's interpretation of the 'medical equivalence' standard for determining disability benefits, arguing that the agency's interpretation was inconsistent with the statutory text and prior case law.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Hargress v. Social Security Administration on October 15, 2017, to address whether the Social Security Administration's interpretation of its own regulations regarding medical equivalence was reasonable and entitled to deference.

Prior to 2018, the Supreme Court had a history of upholding agency interpretations of their own regulations unless those interpretations were plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation, as seen in cases like Christensen v. Harris County (2000).

The Social Security Administration's regulations regarding medical equivalence are complex and often require the agency to make subjective judgments about whether a claimant's condition is medically equivalent to a listed impairment, a process that has historically been afforded significant deference by the courts.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Walker v. Beaumont Independent School District on October 1, 2019, to review the Fifth Circuit's decision regarding the scope of the ministerial exception.

In Hosanna-Tabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & School v. EEOC (2012), the Supreme Court unanimously recognized the ministerial exception, holding that the First Amendment bars civil courts from adjudicating employment discrimination claims brought by ministers against their religious employers.

In Hosanna-Tabor, the Court established a functional test for determining ministerial status, considering factors such as the employee's title, the substance of their duties, and the role they play in the religious organization's mission.

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, in the case below the Supreme Court review, held that the plaintiff, a high school teacher who was not ordained and whose primary duties were secular, did not qualify as a minister under the exception, thereby allowing the employment discrimination claim to proceed.

The Supreme Court has historically interpreted the First Amendment's Religion Clauses to provide broad protection to religious institutions regarding their internal governance and selection of personnel, as seen in cases like Corporation of the Presiding Bishop v. Amos (1987).

The facts of the Walker case involve a teacher at a religious school who was fired, and the central legal question is whether the ministerial exception applies to a teacher who performs significant religious duties despite not having an ordained title.

In Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022), the Supreme Court held that the Free Exercise Clause protects religious expression, including prayer, from government interference, rejecting the Lemon test's establishment of a strict separationist approach in favor of a historical practice and understanding analysis.

In Carson v. Makin (2022), the Supreme Court ruled that a state cannot exclude religious schools from a tuition assistance program solely because of their religious character, establishing that the Free Exercise Clause prohibits discrimination against religion based on its status.

In Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission (2018), the Supreme Court held that government bodies must maintain neutrality toward religion and cannot display hostility toward religious beliefs when enforcing generally applicable laws.

In Town of Greece v. Galloway (2014), the Supreme Court held that legislative prayer is consistent with the First Amendment's Establishment Clause as long as it does not coerce participation and follows historical tradition, indicating a broad protection for religious expression in public forums.

In Walker v. Texas Division, Sons of Confederate Veterans (2015), the Supreme Court held that specialty license plates are government speech, allowing the state to reject messages it disagrees with, but this exception is narrow and does not apply to traditional public forums like sidewalks or parks.

In Reed v. Town of Gilbert (2015), the Supreme Court established that content-based restrictions on speech are subject to strict scrutiny, requiring the government to prove the regulation is narrowly tailored to serve a compelling state interest.

In City of Ladue v. Gilleo (1994), the Supreme Court struck down a ban on residential signs, emphasizing that the First Amendment protects the right to communicate ideas through signs in one's own yard, a traditional public forum for speech.

In Watchtower Bible & Tract Society of New York, Inc. v. Village of Stratton (2002), the Supreme Court held that a municipal ordinance requiring a permit for door-to-door advocacy was unconstitutional because it imposed a prior restraint on speech without sufficient narrow tailoring.

In Reilly v. City of Chicago (2023), the Seventh Circuit (and similar lower courts) have increasingly applied strict scrutiny to ordinances that restrict religious expression or impose permit requirements on religious activities in public spaces, often finding them unconstitutional under the First Amendment.

The Supreme Court has consistently ruled that the government cannot discriminate against religious speakers or impose burdens on religious exercise that are not applied to secular speakers in a comparable manner, as seen in cases like Lamb's Chapel v. Center Moriches Union Free School District (1993).

In 2017, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in Edmo v. Corizon, Inc. that the deliberate indifference standard of the Eighth Amendment applies to transgender prisoners seeking gender-affirming surgery, and that the district court's finding that the prison officials were deliberately indifferent was supported by the record.

The Supreme Court of the United States has established in Estelle v. Gamble (1976) that deliberate indifference to serious medical needs of prisoners constitutes cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment.

In 2018, the Ninth Circuit denied a petition for rehearing en banc in Edmo v. Corizon, Inc., with a dissenting opinion arguing that the majority's decision expanded the definition of serious medical needs beyond established precedent.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Edmo v. Corizon, Inc. on October 1, 2018, to review the Ninth Circuit's decision regarding the standard for deliberate indifference in the context of gender dysphoria treatment.

Prior to 2019, the Supreme Court had not issued a definitive ruling on whether gender dysphoria constitutes a serious medical need requiring specific treatment like surgery under the Eighth Amendment, though lower courts were increasingly recognizing it as such.

The petitioner (Idaho Department of Corrections and Corizon) argued that the Ninth Circuit's decision created a circuit split and improperly expanded the Eighth Amendment to mandate specific medical treatments not previously recognized as constitutionally required.

The respondent (Adree Edmo) argued that the Ninth Circuit correctly applied the deliberate indifference standard and that the evidence showed prison officials ignored clear medical consensus regarding the necessity of surgery for her condition.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Evenwel v. Abbott to determine whether the Equal Protection Clause requires state legislative districts to be drawn based on total population or eligible voter population.

In Reynolds v. Sims (1964), the Supreme Court established the 'one person, one vote' principle, holding that the Equal Protection Clause requires state legislative districts to be substantially equal in population.

In Burns v. Richardson (1966), the Supreme Court held that the Equal Protection Clause does not prohibit states from using a voter registration base for apportionment if the state legislature chooses to do so, but it did not mandate such a base.

In Avery v. Midland County (1968), the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the Equal Protection Clause requires legislative districts to be apportioned on a population basis, but did not specify that the population must be limited to eligible voters.

The Supreme Court has historically allowed states to use total population for apportionment, as seen in the practice of using census data which counts all persons regardless of citizenship or voting eligibility.

In Evenwel v. Abbott, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the use of total population for drawing state legislative districts, citing the long-standing practice and the text of the Constitution.
The Supreme Court has previously indicated in cases like Evenwel that the choice of population base is a matter of state policy, provided it does not discriminate against voters.

In Graham v. Connor (1989), the Supreme Court held that all claims that a law enforcement officer's use of force during an arrest, investigatory stop, or other seizure of a free citizen are properly analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's 'objective reasonableness' standard, rather than under a substantive due process standard.

In Kingsley v. Hendrickson (2015), the Supreme Court held that a pretrial detainee's excessive force claim under the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause requires proof that the officer acted with subjective intent to harm, but the standard for the force itself is objective reasonableness from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene.

In Kingsley v. Hendrickson (2015), the Court explicitly rejected the argument that a pretrial detainee must prove the officer acted with a 'malicious and sadistic' intent to cause harm, a standard previously applied in some circuits under the substantive due process clause.

In Albright v. Oliver (1998), the Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause does not provide a cause of action for a pretrial detainee alleging that their pretrial detention was based on insufficient evidence, as such claims are properly analyzed under the Fourth Amendment.

In Bell v. Wolfish (1979), the Supreme Court established that conditions of confinement for pretrial detainees are evaluated under the Due Process Clause, prohibiting punishment but allowing for reasonable restrictions necessary for security and order.

In Kingsley v. Hendrickson (2015), the Court clarified that the standard for excessive force claims by pretrial detainees is objective reasonableness, meaning the force used must be objectively reasonable in light of the facts and circumstances confronting the officer, without regard to whether the officer had a bad intent.

In Saucier v. Katz (2001), the Supreme Court established the two-step qualified immunity analysis: first, whether the facts alleged show a violation of a constitutional right, and second, whether that right was clearly established at the time of the incident.

In Pearson v. Callahan (2009), the Supreme Court held that lower courts have discretion to decide whether to address the qualified immunity defense before addressing the constitutional violation, often leading to dismissals on immunity grounds if the right was not clearly established.

In 2017, the Social Security Administration (SSA) issued a final rule changing the standard for evaluating medical opinions from claimants, shifting from the 'treating physician rule' to a new standard that gives less weight to treating sources and more weight to the persuasiveness of the evidence.

In 2019, the SSA issued a final rule further clarifying the evaluation of medical opinions, specifically stating that the weight given to a medical source's opinion is determined by the source's supportability and consistency, rather than the source's relationship to the claimant.

In Kisor v. Wilkie (2019), the Supreme Court held that while agencies are entitled to deference under Auer v. Robbins, such deference is limited to situations where the regulation is genuinely ambiguous and the agency's interpretation is reasonable, and the interpretation must reflect the agency's authoritative position.

In 2020, the D.C. Circuit in Kaufmann v. Saul (later Kaufmann v. Kijakazi) vacated the SSA's 2017 and 2019 rules, holding that the rules were arbitrary and capricious because they conflicted with the Social Security Act's requirement that the Commissioner consider the treating physician's opinion and that the rules were not supported by substantial evidence.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Kaufmann v. Kijakazi on October 15, 2021, to resolve a circuit split regarding the validity of the SSA's 2017 and 2019 rules and the standard of review for agency interpretations of the Social Security Act.

In 2021, the Supreme Court in Bostock v. Clayton County clarified that statutory interpretation requires looking at the plain text of the statute, and that agency interpretations cannot override clear statutory text.

The Social Security Act explicitly requires the Commissioner to consider the treating physician's opinion and gives it controlling weight if it is well-supported and not inconsistent with other evidence in the record.

In 2019, the Supreme Court decided Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, holding that a plaintiff must demonstrate a concrete injury-in-fact to satisfy Article III standing, even when a statute grants a right to sue and provides for statutory damages.

In 2021, the Supreme Court decided TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, holding that a bare procedural violation of a federal statute, without any accompanying concrete harm, does not constitute an injury-in-fact sufficient for Article III standing.

The case involves a dispute over the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Airworthiness Directives (ADs) and whether the plaintiffs, who purchased aircraft engines, have standing to sue for alleged violations of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act and state consumer protection laws based on the failure to comply with these ADs.

The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, in a decision prior to the Supreme Court's grant of certiorari, held that the plaintiffs had standing because the alleged violations of the ADs created a risk of harm that was sufficiently concrete, or that the statutory violations themselves constituted a concrete injury.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in LNS Enterprises LLC v. Continental Motors, Inc. on October 1, 2021, to resolve a circuit split regarding the application of standing principles in cases involving statutory violations of federal safety regulations.

Prior to 2022, the Supreme Court had consistently narrowed the scope of Article III standing in cases involving statutory violations where no tangible harm was alleged, as seen in Spokeo and TransUnion.

The Unclaimed Property Act of 1981 (UPA) establishes a priority scheme for escheating unclaimed property, placing the state of the last known address of the holder of the property at the top of the priority list.

In Texas v. New Jersey (1965), the Supreme Court established the primary rule that the state of the last known address of the creditor (holder) has the right to escheat unclaimed property, subject to the condition that the state must have a valid claim under its own laws.

In Texas v. New Jersey (1965), the Supreme Court established a secondary rule: if the state of the last known address has no valid claim to the property under its own laws, the property may be escheated to the state of the holder's principal place of business.

In Texas v. New Jersey (1965), the Supreme Court established a tertiary rule: if neither the state of the last known address nor the state of the holder's principal place of business has a valid claim, the property may be escheated to the state of the holder's domicile.

In Delaware v. New York (1996), the Supreme Court held that the state of the last known address rule applies to uncashed checks and other financial instruments, and that the state of the holder's principal place of business is the fallback only if the last known address state has no valid claim.

In Texas v. New Jersey (1965), the Court noted that the priority rules are designed to prevent multiple states from claiming the same property and to provide a clear, uniform rule for the escheat of intangible property.

In Texas v. New Jersey (1965), the Court explicitly stated that the state of the last known address rule is the primary rule and that the state of the holder's principal place of business is a secondary rule to be applied only when the primary rule cannot be satisfied.

In Texas v. New Jersey (1965), the Court held that the state of the last known address rule applies even if the holder has no physical presence in that state, provided the state has a valid claim under its own laws.

In Whole Woman's Health v. Hellerstedt (2016), the Supreme Court held that abortion regulations must not place a substantial obstacle in the path of a woman seeking an abortion before fetal viability, applying an undue burden standard.

In Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), the Supreme Court established the undue burden standard for evaluating abortion restrictions, holding that states may regulate abortion before viability as long as the regulation does not place a substantial obstacle in the path of a woman seeking an abortion.
In Stenberg v. Carhart (2000), the Supreme Court struck down a Nebraska law banning 'partial-birth' abortion because the law lacked an exception for the health of the mother and was overly broad.

In Gonzales v. Carhart (2007), the Supreme Court upheld the federal Partial-Birth Abortion Ban Act of 2003, distinguishing it from the law in Stenberg by noting the federal law included an exception for the life of the mother and was not overly broad.

The Indiana law at issue (HB 2) banned abortions based on the race, sex, or disability of the fetus, including those with a diagnosis of Down syndrome, and contained no exception for the health of the mother.

In June Medical Services L.L.C. v. Russo (2020), the Court struck down a Louisiana law requiring abortion providers to have admitting privileges at nearby hospitals, reaffirming the undue burden standard and the requirement for health exceptions.

The Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals, in Planned Parenthood of Indiana and Kentucky, Inc. v. Box (2018), upheld a preliminary injunction against the Indiana law, finding that the lack of a health exception and the broad ban on disability-based abortions likely violated the undue burden standard.

In McCullen v. Coakley (2014), the Supreme Court struck down a Massachusetts law creating buffer zones around abortion clinics, emphasizing that the government must use the least restrictive means to achieve its interests when regulating abortion.

In 2017, Congress enacted the PACT Act, which expanded the scope of presumptive service connection for veterans exposed to toxic substances, including burn pits, and was intended to address the long-standing gap in benefits for veterans exposed to such hazards.

The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) has historically interpreted the statutory requirement for 'active military, naval, or air service' to exclude service performed in a non-combatant capacity or service that did not involve specific types of hazardous exposure unless explicitly listed in regulations.

In *Kisor v. Wilkie* (2019), the Supreme Court held that while agencies retain some deference in interpreting ambiguous regulations, courts must first exhaust all standard tools of construction before deferring to an agency's interpretation, and deference is only appropriate if the regulation is genuinely ambiguous and the agency's interpretation is reasonable.

In *Bostock v. Clayton County* (2020), the Supreme Court ruled that statutory terms must be interpreted according to their ordinary meaning at the time of enactment, emphasizing a textualist approach over agency policy preferences when the text is clear.

The Federal Circuit, in *Rudisill v. Wilkie* (2021), affirmed the VA's denial of benefits, holding that the statutory language regarding 'active service' did not encompass the specific type of service performed by the petitioner in a non-combatant role prior to the PACT Act's expansion, relying on the VA's regulatory interpretation.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in *Rudisill v. McDonough* to determine whether the VA's interpretation of the statutory term 'active military, naval, or air service' was correct, specifically regarding whether service in a non-combatant capacity qualifies for presumptive benefits under the relevant statutes.

In *Gundy v. United States* (2019), the Court addressed the scope of the non-delegation doctrine but did not resolve the broader question of agency deference in statutory interpretation, leaving the *Chevron* framework (prior to its potential overturning) or *Skidmore* deference as the governing standards for agency statutory interpretation.

The PACT Act of 2022 (enacted after the lower court decision but before the Supreme Court's term) explicitly expanded the list of toxic exposures and service periods, suggesting a legislative intent to broaden coverage, which may influence the Court's view on the statutory interpretation of the pre-2022 law.

In United States v. Tinker (2021), the Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Ninth Circuit's decision regarding the constitutionality of the federal statute prohibiting felons from possessing firearms.

The Ninth Circuit held in United States v. Tinker that the federal felon-in-possession statute (18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1)) is unconstitutional as applied to the petitioner because he was a non-violent felon and the statute lacked a mens rea requirement for the possession element.

In United States v. Miller (1939), the Supreme Court held that the Second Amendment protects the right to keep and bear arms only in the context of militia service, a standard that was later modified but established a historical tradition framework.

In District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), the Supreme Court held that the Second Amendment protects an individual's right to possess firearms for self-defense within the home, but also explicitly stated that the right is not unlimited and that long-standing prohibitions on the possession of firearms by felons are presumptively lawful.

In McDonald v. City of Chicago (2010), the Supreme Court incorporated the Second Amendment against the states, reaffirming the individual right to keep and bear arms while noting that the right is subject to reasonable regulation.

In United States v. Chester (2010), the Fourth Circuit upheld the constitutionality of 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) as applied to a felon, relying on the historical tradition of disarming dangerous individuals.

In United States v. Skoien (2010), the Seventh Circuit upheld the constitutionality of the felon-in-possession statute, emphasizing that the government has a compelling interest in preventing gun violence.

In United States v. Chester (2010), the Fourth Circuit noted that the Supreme Court in Heller explicitly listed 'prohibitions on the possession of firearms by felons' as a 'presumptively lawful' regulation.

In United States v. Tinker, the Ninth Circuit's decision was a departure from the consensus of other circuits which had consistently upheld the felon-in-possession statute against Second Amendment challenges.

The Supreme Court has historically been reluctant to strike down federal statutes that have been consistently upheld by lower courts and are based on long-standing historical traditions of firearm regulation.

In 2019, the Supreme Court decided National Labor Relations Board v. Murphy Oil USA, Inc., holding that pre-dispute arbitration agreements requiring employees to waive their right to pursue class or collective actions in the National Labor Relations Act context are unenforceable under the Federal Arbitration Act's saving clause.

In 2018, the Supreme Court decided Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis, holding that the National Labor Relations Act does not override the Federal Arbitration Act, and that arbitration agreements requiring individual arbitration are enforceable even if they waive class or collective actions.

The Supreme Court has consistently held that the Federal Arbitration Act mandates the enforcement of arbitration agreements according to their terms, including provisions for individualized proceedings, unless there are specific grounds under state or federal law for revocation of a contract.

In the case of Levone Harris v. KM Industrial, Inc., the petitioner (KM Industrial) sought review of a lower court decision that likely enforced an arbitration agreement or addressed the enforceability of a class action waiver in an employment dispute, following the precedent set in Epic Systems.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Levone Harris v. KM Industrial, Inc. during the October 2019 term, with the case being argued in early 2020, focusing on the enforceability of arbitration agreements under the Federal Arbitration Act in the context of employment disputes.

In 2023, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of Chinyere Ogbonna-McGruder's Title IX and First Amendment claims against Austin Peay State University, ruling that the university's actions were protected by qualified immunity and that the university had not violated Title IX because the student was not subjected to a hostile environment or denied educational benefits based on sex.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Ogbonna-McGruder v. Austin Peay State University on October 6, 2023, to review whether the Sixth Circuit correctly applied the standard for Title IX liability and qualified immunity in the context of a student's sexual harassment complaint against university officials.

In Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education (1999), the Supreme Court held that a school district is liable under Title IX for student-on-student harassment only if the district is deliberately indifferent to known acts of harassment that are so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that they effectively deny the victim access to an educational opportunity or benefit.

In Hope v. Pelzer (2003), the Supreme Court clarified that qualified immunity protects government officials unless their conduct violates clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known.

In 2022, the Supreme Court decided Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, emphasizing a more rigorous scrutiny of government actions involving religious expression and signaling a shift toward a more textually grounded approach to First Amendment claims, though the case did not directly address Title IX or qualified immunity in the context of student harassment.

The Sixth Circuit's decision in Ogbonna-McGruder relied heavily on the finding that the university officials acted within the scope of their duties and that no clearly established law prohibited their specific conduct at the time, thus granting them qualified immunity.

In United States v. Aruda, the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the district court's judgment, holding that the defendant's sentence was substantively reasonable and that the district court did not abuse its discretion in imposing a sentence within the Guidelines range despite the defendant's arguments regarding the severity of the sentence relative to her role.

The Supreme Court has established that it generally grants certiorari only when there is a conflict among the federal circuit courts or a significant question of federal law, rather than to correct errors in the application of law to specific facts in a single case.

In cases involving sentencing appeals, the Supreme Court has historically been reluctant to intervene unless the sentencing court's decision involves a clear error of law or a departure from established sentencing principles that affects the uniformity of federal sentencing.

The Seventh Circuit's decision in Aruda was based on a review of the district court's findings regarding the defendant's acceptance of responsibility and the specific circumstances of her offense, concluding that the sentence was not an abuse of discretion.

The Supreme Court's docket for the 2020-2021 term included a limited number of criminal sentencing cases, and the Court typically denies certiorari in cases where the lower court's decision is consistent with existing precedent and does not present a novel legal question.

In Nijhawan v. Holder (2009), the Supreme Court held that the 'aggravated felony' definition in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) includes a 'circumstance-specific' element for the theft offense, requiring a specific amount of loss to be proven, rather than just the generic statutory definition.

In Moncrieffe v. Holder (2013), the Supreme Court applied the categorical approach to determine if a state conviction qualifies as an aggravated felony, ruling that the offense must necessarily involve a specific amount of loss or a specific circumstance to match the federal definition.

In Mathis v. United States (2016), the Supreme Court clarified that the categorical approach requires looking only at the statutory elements of the prior offense, not the specific facts of the defendant's conduct, unless the statute is divisible.

In Pugin v. Garland, the petitioner argued that his prior Louisiana conviction for theft of a firearm did not qualify as an 'aggravated felony' under the INA because the state statute did not require proof of a specific amount of loss or value, and the record did not show the firearm's value exceeded the federal threshold.

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, in a decision prior to the Supreme Court's grant of certiorari, held that the petitioner's conviction qualified as an aggravated felony, relying on the fact that the firearm had a value exceeding the federal threshold, despite the lack of a specific finding in the state judgment.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Pugin v. Garland to resolve a circuit split regarding whether the 'circumstance-specific' element of the theft aggravated felony requires a specific finding of the amount of loss in the record of conviction, or if it can be inferred from the nature of the property involved.

In United States v. Leon (1984), the Supreme Court established the good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule, holding that evidence obtained by police officers acting in objectively reasonable reliance on a search warrant later found to be invalid is admissible in criminal proceedings.

In Davis v. United States (2011), the Supreme Court held that the exclusionary rule does not apply when police conduct a search in objectively reasonable reliance on binding appellate precedent that is later overruled.

In Herring v. United States (2009), the Supreme Court ruled that the exclusionary rule applies only where the police conduct is sufficiently deliberate that exclusion can meaningfully deter it, and that isolated negligence does not warrant suppression of evidence.

In Hudson v. Michigan (2006), the Supreme Court held that the exclusionary rule is a last resort and should not be applied where the social costs of exclusion outweigh the benefits, particularly in cases involving knock-and-announce violations.

The Supreme Court has consistently limited the scope of the exclusionary rule in the 21st century, emphasizing that it is not a personal right but a judicially created remedy designed to deter Fourth Amendment violations by law enforcement.

In United States v. Hensley (1985), the Court held that officers may rely on a warrantless arrest warrant if they have reasonable grounds to believe the suspect is a fugitive, even if the warrant was issued based on a minor procedural error, provided the error was not deliberate.

In Illinois v. Krull (1987), the Supreme Court extended the good-faith exception to situations where officers rely on a statute that is subsequently declared unconstitutional, provided the reliance was objectively reasonable.
The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) provides for judicial review of final agency action, but only if the action is 'final' and the plaintiff has standing.

In Sackett v. EPA (2012), the Supreme Court held that a compliance order issued by the EPA under the Clean Water Act was a final agency action subject to judicial review because it determined rights and obligations and marked the consummation of the agency's decision-making process.

In Sackett v. EPA (2012), the Court also held that the Sacketts had standing to challenge the order because they faced a realistic threat of enforcement and significant economic burden if they complied with the order or faced potential penalties.

The Army Corps of Engineers issued a Jurisdictional Determination (JD) to Hawkes Co., Inc., stating that the company's property contained 'waters of the United States' and was therefore subject to the Clean Water Act's permit requirements.

The Corps of Engineers argued that the JD was not a final agency action because it was merely a preliminary step in the permitting process and did not itself impose any legal obligations or penalties.

The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals held that the JD was a final agency action because it determined the legal status of the property and had direct and immediate consequences for the landowner, who would otherwise face significant costs to obtain a permit or risk enforcement.

In Bennett v. Spear (1997), the Supreme Court defined 'final agency action' as action that marks the consummation of the agency's decision-making process and is one by which rights or obligations have been determined or from which legal consequences will flow.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in United States Army Corps of Engineers v. Hawkes Co., Inc. to resolve a circuit split regarding whether a Jurisdictional Determination under the Clean Water Act constitutes final agency action.

In Bostock v. Clayton County, Georgia, the Supreme Court granted certiorari to address whether Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits employment discrimination 'because of... sex', covers discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

In R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes Inc. v. EEOC, the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals held that Title VII's prohibition on sex discrimination encompasses discrimination based on gender identity, affirming the EEOC's interpretation.

In Oncale v. Sundowner Offshore Services, Inc., the Supreme Court held that Title VII's prohibition on sex discrimination extends to same-sex harassment, establishing that the statute covers discrimination based on sex regardless of the gender of the parties involved.
In Price Waterhouse v. Hopkins, the Supreme Court held that discrimination based on failure to conform to gender stereotypes constitutes discrimination 'because of sex' under Title VII.

The Supreme Court has historically interpreted the phrase 'because of sex' in Title VII broadly to include any employment action where sex is a motivating factor, as seen in cases like Los Angeles Dept. of Water & Power v. Manhart.

The EEOC issued a decision in 2012 (Macy v. Holder) and a 2015 decision in Baldwin v. Foxx, concluding that discrimination based on gender identity and sexual orientation is inherently discrimination because of sex under Title VII.

In the Harris Funeral Homes case, the petitioner argued that the EEOC's interpretation was an overreach and that Title VII does not cover gender identity, while the respondent argued that firing an employee for transitioning is a direct result of their sex.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in the Harris Funeral Homes case to be decided alongside Bostock v. Clayton County and Altitude Express v. Zarda, consolidating the legal questions regarding Title VII and LGBTQ+ discrimination.

In Pearson v. Callahan (2009), the Supreme Court held that the qualified immunity analysis is no longer strictly sequential, allowing courts to decide whether a constitutional right was clearly established without first determining if a right existed.

In Saucier v. Katz (2001), the Supreme Court established a mandatory two-step sequence for qualified immunity: first determine if a constitutional right was violated, then determine if that right was clearly established.

In Harlow v. Fitzgerald (1982), the Supreme Court held that government officials performing discretionary functions are generally shielded from liability for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known.

In Anderson v. Creighton (1987), the Supreme Court clarified that the 'clearly established' standard requires that the contours of the right be sufficiently clear that a reasonable official would understand that what he is doing violates that right.

In Mullenix v. Luna (2015), the Supreme Court reversed a lower court's denial of qualified immunity, emphasizing that the clearly established law must be particularized to the facts of the case, not stated at a high level of generality.

In Kisela v. Hughes (2018), the Supreme Court unanimously reversed a Ninth Circuit decision denying qualified immunity to an officer who shot a woman, holding that the law was not clearly established that the officer's use of force was unconstitutional under the specific circumstances.

In City of Escondido v. Emmons (2019), the Supreme Court vacated a lower court decision and remanded for reconsideration in light of Kisela, reinforcing the strict application of the clearly established standard in qualified immunity cases.

In the context of the 2022 term, the Supreme Court had not yet issued a decision in Clark v. Coupe as of the cutoff date, but the case involved a claim of excessive force and qualified immunity for law enforcement officers.
In Whren v. United States (1996), the Supreme Court held that the subjective intentions of police officers do not invalidate an otherwise objectively reasonable stop under the Fourth Amendment.

In United States v. Arvizu (2002), the Supreme Court ruled that the reasonableness of a seizure is judged by the totality of the circumstances, allowing for inferences that might be mistaken but are reasonable under the circumstances.

In Illinois v. Rodriguez (1990), the Supreme Court established that a warrantless search is valid if the police reasonably believe the person consenting has authority, even if that belief is mistaken.

In Maryland v. Wilson (1997), the Supreme Court held that police officers may order passengers out of a vehicle during a traffic stop as a matter of course for officer safety, emphasizing the practical realities of policing.
In Terry v. Ohio (1968), the Supreme Court established that a stop is reasonable if based on specific and articulable facts that, taken together with rational inferences, warrant the intrusion.

In Heien v. North Carolina, the North Carolina Court of Appeals had previously held that a police officer's reasonable mistake of law regarding a vehicle equipment statute could justify a stop under the Fourth Amendment.

The Supreme Court has historically distinguished between mistakes of fact and mistakes of law, generally holding that a mistake of law does not justify a seizure, as seen in cases like United States v. Leon (1984) regarding the good faith exception to the exclusionary rule which applies to warrants, not necessarily to the initial seizure justification.

In Social Security Ruling 96-9p, the Social Security Administration established that an Administrative Law Judge must provide specific reasons for rejecting a treating physician's opinion, and if the ALJ rejects it, they must provide clear and convincing reasons or specific and legitimate reasons that are substantial.

In Andrews v. Astrue, 536 F.3d 1033 (9th Cir. 2008), the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held that an ALJ's failure to provide specific and legitimate reasons for rejecting a treating physician's opinion constitutes reversible error.

In Molina v. Astrue, 674 F.3d 1104 (9th Cir. 2012), the Ninth Circuit clarified that an ALJ's failure to properly weigh a treating physician's opinion, particularly when the ALJ relies on a non-examining physician's opinion without sufficient justification, requires remand.

In Berryhill v. Yancey, 828 F.3d 1007 (9th Cir. 2016), the Ninth Circuit reversed a district court's affirmation of an ALJ's decision where the ALJ failed to provide specific and legitimate reasons for rejecting the opinions of treating and examining physicians.

In the case of Luther v. Berryhill, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals issued an opinion on March 2, 2018, affirming the district court's decision to reverse the ALJ's denial of benefits, finding that the ALJ failed to provide specific and legitimate reasons for rejecting the treating physician's opinion.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Luther v. Berryhill on October 1, 2018, to resolve a circuit split regarding the standard of review for an ALJ's rejection of a treating physician's opinion, specifically whether the 'specific and legitimate reasons' standard applies or if a more deferential standard is appropriate.

In United States v. Booker (2005), the Supreme Court held that the Federal Sentencing Guidelines are advisory, not mandatory, and that appellate courts must review sentences for reasonableness under an abuse of discretion standard.

In Gall v. United States (2007), the Supreme Court established that appellate courts must review all sentences—both inside and outside the Guidelines range—under a deferential abuse of discretion standard, requiring a careful consideration of the totality of the circumstances.

In Rita v. United States (2007), the Supreme Court held that appellate courts may apply a presumption of reasonableness to sentences within the properly calculated Guidelines range, but this presumption is not binding and does not alter the abuse of discretion standard of review.

In Koons v. United States (2018), the Supreme Court held that a defendant who receives a sentence below the statutory minimum under 18 U.S.C. § 3553(e) or the safety valve provision is not entitled to a downward departure based on a change in law or policy after the sentence was imposed, unless the change is retroactive.

In United States v. Booker, the Court clarified that the Sixth Amendment right to a jury trial does not apply to the determination of sentencing factors that increase a sentence beyond the statutory maximum, provided the sentence is within the statutory range.

In Pepper v. United States (2011), the Supreme Court held that a district court may consider evidence of post-sentencing rehabilitation when reviewing a sentence on remand, but this does not create a general right to modify a final sentence based on changed circumstances without a statutory basis.

In Irizarry v. United States (2008), the Supreme Court held that a district court is not required to provide notice to the parties that it intends to impose a sentence outside the Guidelines range, provided the court considers the parties' arguments and the § 3553(a) factors.

In United States v. Booker, the Court established that the Federal Sentencing Guidelines are advisory, and appellate courts must review sentences for reasonableness under an abuse of discretion standard.

In Graham v. Connor (1989), the Supreme Court established that all claims that a citizen was subjected to excessive force in the course of an arrest, investigatory stop, or other seizure of a free citizen should be analyzed under the Fourth Amendment and its 'reasonableness' standard rather than under a substantive due process standard.

In Tennessee v. Garner (1985), the Supreme Court held that the use of deadly force to prevent the escape of a fleeing suspect is only reasonable if the officer has probable cause to believe that the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others.

In Scott v. Harris (2007), the Supreme Court ruled that a police officer's use of deadly force to terminate a high-speed vehicle chase is reasonable under the Fourth Amendment when the suspect poses a significant threat to the public, even if the suspect is not armed.

In Saucier v. Katz (2001), the Supreme Court established the two-step qualified immunity analysis: first, whether the facts alleged show the officer's conduct violated a constitutional right, and second, whether that right was clearly established at the time of the incident.

In Pearson v. Callahan (2009), the Supreme Court held that the two-step qualified immunity analysis from Saucier is discretionary, allowing courts to decide whether to address the constitutional violation or the clearly established law prong first.

In Plumhoff v. Rickard (2014), the Supreme Court held that the use of deadly force to end a dangerous vehicle chase was reasonable where the suspect's driving posed a grave risk to the public and the officers' actions were necessary to stop the threat.

In Mullenix v. Luna (2015), the Supreme Court affirmed that an officer is not liable for a split-second decision to use deadly force during a high-speed chase if the officer's actions were objectively reasonable under the circumstances, even if a different officer might have chosen a different tactic.

In City of Los Angeles v. Mendez (2017), the Supreme Court clarified that the 'totality of the circumstances' test for excessive force does not require a separate analysis of whether the officer's actions were 'provoked' by the suspect's conduct, but rather focuses on the reasonableness of the force used in light of the threat posed.

In Abood v. Detroit Board of Education (1977), the Supreme Court held that public sector unions could charge non-members an agency fee to cover collective bargaining costs, but could not use those fees for political or ideological purposes without the non-member's consent.

In Knox v. Service Employees International Union Local 1000 (2012), the Court ruled that unions must obtain affirmative consent from non-members before charging them for special assessments or dues increases used for political purposes, signaling a shift toward stricter scrutiny of compelled speech in the union context.

In Harris v. Quinn (2014), the Court held that home health care providers who were not full union members could not be compelled to pay agency fees, distinguishing them from full public employees and suggesting that the Abood precedent might be limited or overruled.

In McCutcheon v. Federal Election Commission (2014), the Court emphasized that the government has a compelling interest in preventing corruption but that the First Amendment protects the right to refrain from speaking, including the right not to subsidize speech one disagrees with.

In Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010), the Court held that the government cannot restrict independent political expenditures by corporations and unions, reinforcing the principle that political speech is protected regardless of the speaker's identity and that compelled funding of such speech is suspect.

In Janus v. AFSCME, the petitioner argued that mandatory agency fees for public sector unions violate the First Amendment's Free Speech Clause because collective bargaining in the public sector is inherently political and compelled fees force employees to subsidize speech they may oppose.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Janus v. AFSCME specifically to reconsider the constitutionality of Abood v. Detroit Board of Education, indicating the Court's willingness to potentially overturn a decades-old precedent.

In recent years, the composition of the Supreme Court has shifted toward a more conservative majority, with the appointment of Justice Gorsuch in 2017, which has been associated with a trend of limiting government-compelled speech and expanding First Amendment protections in cases involving unions and political spending.

In Estelle v. Smith (1981), the Supreme Court held that the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination applies to pre-trial psychiatric examinations conducted for the purpose of determining a defendant's sanity or future dangerousness, and that statements made during such examinations cannot be used against the defendant at the sentencing phase without prior warning.

In Ake v. Oklahoma (1985), the Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires the state to provide a defendant with access to a psychiatric expert if the defendant's sanity is likely to be a significant factor at the trial, and this right extends to the sentencing phase in capital cases where the defendant's mental state is relevant.

In Barefoot v. Estelle (1983), the Supreme Court held that the use of psychiatric testimony to predict future dangerousness in capital sentencing does not violate the Due Process Clause, provided the testimony is based on reliable methods and the defendant has the opportunity to cross-examine the expert.

In Strickland v. Washington (1984), the Supreme Court established the two-prong test for ineffective assistance of counsel: the defendant must show that counsel's performance was deficient and that the deficiency prejudiced the defense, meaning there is a reasonable probability that, but for counsel's unprofessional errors, the result of the proceeding would have been different.

In Wiggins v. Smith (2003), the Supreme Court held that counsel's failure to investigate and present mitigating evidence regarding the defendant's traumatic background and mental health history constituted ineffective assistance of counsel under the Strickland standard.

In Rompilla v. Beard (2005), the Supreme Court held that counsel's failure to review readily available files containing the defendant's prior criminal record and mental health history, which could have provided significant mitigating evidence, was deficient performance under Strickland.

In McWilliams v. Dunn, the petitioner argued that the state's failure to provide a defense expert to assist in evaluating his mental state for the sentencing phase, despite the state's own expert testifying for the prosecution, violated the Due Process Clause as interpreted in Ake v. Oklahoma.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals, in its decision on McWilliams v. Dunn, held that Ake v. Oklahoma only requires the state to provide a psychiatrist to assist the defense in evaluating the defendant's mental state, but does not require the state to provide a psychiatrist to assist the defense in presenting mitigating evidence or to provide a defense expert if the state has already provided one for its own purposes.

In 2015, the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals in Guertin v. City of Flint held that the City of Flint and its officials were liable under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for violating the Due Process Clause by exposing residents to lead-contaminated water, rejecting qualified immunity for officials who knew of the danger and failed to act.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Shari Guertin v. State of Michigan on October 2, 2018, to review the Sixth Circuit's decision regarding the scope of qualified immunity and the liability of state and local officials in the Flint water crisis.

Under the qualified immunity doctrine established in Harlow v. Fitzgerald (1982), government officials are immune from civil liability unless their conduct violated clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known.

In City of Ontario v. Quon (2010), the Supreme Court emphasized that qualified immunity is a robust defense intended to protect officials from the burdens of litigation, requiring that the unlawfulness of the conduct be apparent in light of pre-existing law.

In Mullenix v. Luna (2015), the Supreme Court reversed a lower court's denial of qualified immunity, holding that the law was not clearly established at the time of the incident, thereby reinforcing the high bar for overcoming qualified immunity.

The Sixth Circuit in Guertin found that the right to be free from exposure to lead-contaminated water was clearly established under the Due Process Clause, relying on prior case law regarding the state's affirmative duty to protect citizens from known dangers.

The Supreme Court's docket for the 2018-2019 term included arguments on qualified immunity cases where the Court had shown a tendency to narrow the scope of liability for officials, as seen in the 2018-2019 term's focus on the 'clearly established' prong.
In 2016, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Alexander Edionwe v. Guy Bailey to review the Fifth Circuit's decision regarding the statute of limitations for Title VII claims.

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals held that the statute of limitations for a Title VII claim begins to run when the employer makes the final decision to terminate the employee, not when the employee receives notice of that decision.

The Supreme Court has previously established in National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Morgan (2002) that the statute of limitations for Title VII claims begins to run when the discriminatory act occurs, not when the effects of that act are felt.

In United States v. Kubrick (1979), the Supreme Court held that the statute of limitations for a claim begins to run when the plaintiff knows or should have known of the injury, even if the plaintiff does not know the full extent of the injury or that it was actionable.

The petitioner, Alexander Edionwe, argued that the statute of limitations should begin when he received notice of the termination decision, as he was unaware of the finality of the decision until that point.
The respondent, Guy Bailey, argued that the statute of limitations began when the university made the final decision to terminate Edionwe, regardless of when Edionwe was notified.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in this case specifically to resolve a circuit split regarding the start date of the statute of limitations for Title VII claims, with the Fifth Circuit's rule differing from other circuits that had adopted the 'notice' rule.

In Baze v. Rees (2008), the Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment prohibits only those methods of execution that involve 'objectively intolerable risk of severe pain' and that a prisoner must show that the risk of severe pain is substantial in comparison to known and available alternatives.

In Glossip v. Gross (2014), the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the district court's denial of the petitioners' claim, finding that the petitioners failed to identify a known and available alternative method of execution that would significantly reduce the risk of severe pain.

The Supreme Court granted certiorari in Glossip v. Gross to determine whether the use of midazolam in lethal injection protocols violates the Eighth Amendment and whether the petitioners met the burden of identifying a known and available alternative method of execution.

In Baze v. Rees, the Court explicitly stated that the Constitution does not require the elimination of all risk of pain, but only the elimination of methods that pose a substantial risk of severe pain compared to alternatives.

The petitioners in Glossip argued that midazolam is an ineffective anesthetic and that other methods, such as a three-drug cocktail or a single dose of pentobarbital, were known and available alternatives.

The Supreme Court has historically been reluctant to second-guess state execution protocols unless there is a clear constitutional violation, as seen in Baze v. Rees and earlier cases like Ford v. Wainwright (1986) regarding the execution of the insane.

In Tennessee v. Garner (1985), the Supreme Court held that the use of deadly force against a fleeing suspect is unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment unless the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others.

In Graham v. Connor (1989), the Supreme Court established that all claims that law enforcement officers have used excessive force in the course of an arrest, investigatory stop, or other seizure of a free citizen should be analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's 'objective reasonableness' standard.

In Saucier v. Katz (2001), the Supreme Court established a two-step qualified immunity analysis: first, whether the facts alleged show the officer's conduct violated a constitutional right, and second, whether that right was clearly established at the time of the incident.

In Pearson v. Callahan (2009), the Supreme Court held that the two-step Saucier sequence is no longer mandatory, allowing courts to decide qualified immunity cases on the ground that the right was not clearly established without first deciding if a constitutional violation occurred.

In Plumhoff v. Rickard (2014), the Supreme Court held that an officer's use of deadly force to stop a dangerous flight is reasonable under the Fourth Amendment when the suspect poses a significant threat to the public, even if the suspect is not armed.

In Mullenix v. Luna (2015), the Supreme Court reversed a lower court's denial of qualified immunity, holding that an officer is entitled to immunity unless the law was so clearly established that every reasonable official would have understood that what he was doing violated the law, emphasizing that the right must be defined with particularity.

In City of Los Angeles v. Mendez (2017), the Supreme Court clarified that the 'clearly established' prong of qualified immunity requires that the unlawfulness of the officer's conduct be apparent in light of pre-existing law, and that the right must be defined in a sufficiently clear and specific manner.

In Kisela v. Hughes (2018), the Supreme Court unanimously reversed a lower court's denial of qualified immunity, holding that the officer was entitled to immunity because the law was not clearly established that shooting a woman who was holding a knife but not threatening anyone immediately was unconstitutional.

In White v. Pauly (2017), the Supreme Court summarily reversed a lower court's denial of qualified immunity, reiterating that qualified immunity protects all but the plainly incompetent or those who violate clearly established law.

In the case of Heeter v. Bowers (6th Cir. 2023), the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the district court's denial of qualified immunity for the police officers, holding that the use of deadly force against a fleeing suspect who was not posing an immediate threat of death or serious physical injury violated clearly established law under Tennessee v. Garner.
In 2018, the Supreme Court granted certiorari in Daugherty v. Harrington to review the Ninth Circuit's decision regarding the scope of qualified immunity for federal officers under Bivens actions.

The Ninth Circuit held in Daugherty v. Harrington that federal officers are entitled to qualified immunity in Bivens actions if their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known.

In Pearson v. Callahan (2009), the Supreme Court held that lower courts have the discretion to decide qualified immunity cases on the basis of whether the right was clearly established without first determining whether a constitutional right was violated.

In Saucier v. Katz (2001), the Supreme Court established a mandatory two-step sequence for qualified immunity analysis: first determine if a constitutional right was violated, then determine if the right was clearly established.

In Ashcroft v. al-Kidd (2011), the Supreme Court reaffirmed that qualified immunity protects officials unless their conduct violates clearly established law, emphasizing the importance of the 'clearly established' prong.

The petitioner, Daugherty, argued that the Ninth Circuit erred by applying qualified immunity to a federal officer's conduct that allegedly violated the Fourth Amendment, contending that the right was clearly established.

The Supreme Court has historically been reluctant to expand Bivens remedies and has often granted qualified immunity to federal officers in novel fact patterns to avoid judicial interference with executive functions.

In 1996, Congress amended the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) to require that plan fiduciaries act solely in the interest of participants and beneficiaries and for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits.
In 2004, the Supreme Court in Varity Corp. v. Howe held that ERISA fiduciaries have a duty of prudence that requires them to monitor investments and remove imprudent ones.

In 2016, the Supreme Court in Hecker v. Deere & Co. held that a plaintiff can state a claim for breach of fiduciary duty by alleging that the plan fiduciaries failed to monitor the investment options or failed to remove imprudent options, even if the plan itself was not imprudent.

In 2018, the Supreme Court in Hughes v. Northwestern University (7th Cir. 2018) affirmed the district court's dismissal, but the Supreme Court granted certiorari in 2020 to review the standard for fiduciary duty regarding investment options.

In 2020, the Supreme Court in Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer held that a plaintiff must plausibly allege an alternative action that a fiduciary could have taken that would not have violated ERISA's duty of prudence, but the Court did not establish a bright-line rule that a plan is automatically prudent if it includes a broad range of options.

In 2021, the Supreme Court in JPMorgan Chase & Co. v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (a related ERISA case) reaffirmed that fiduciaries must consider the costs of investment options and the availability of lower-cost alternatives.
